**The Weight of a Name**

I remember the first time I heard my name spoken aloud. It wasn’t in a mirror, where the sound of it felt like a secret, or in a classroom where it was called out like a roll call. No, it was in the hush of a library at dusk, when the librarian—Mrs. Holloway, with her silver hair and the way she always smelled like old books and cinnamon—turned to me and said, *"You’ve been waiting here for twenty minutes, James."*

I didn’t move. My fingers, still clutching the spine of *The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde*, trembled. The name *James* had been mine for twelve years, but hearing it from her lips made it feel heavier, like a coin in my pocket I’d forgotten to spend.

That was the day I realized names weren’t just labels. They were promises. Or debts. Or both.

---

Years later, I’d forget my own name in a crowd. Not the way you forget a grocery item—no, this was deeper. It happened in a city I didn’t recognize, where the air smelled of exhaust and something sweet, like burnt sugar. I was standing in front of a café with a chalkboard sign that read *"Coffee & Dreams"* in a handwriting that looked like it belonged to someone who’d written it in the dark. I ordered a drink, and when the barista asked for my name, I blinked.

*"What?"*

She tilted her head. *"Your name?"*

I pressed my palms to my temples. *"I don’t know."*

The barista—young, with a tattoo of a crescent moon on her wrist—didn’t laugh. She just slid a cup of coffee toward me and said, *"It’s okay. You’ll remember."*

I didn’t.

---

Names are the first things we lose when we stop being who we were. My mother used to say that, after my father left. She’d sit on the porch swing at night, rocking back and forth, and say it like a prayer. *"Names are the first things we lose."*

I didn’t understand until I was older, until I saw how people could unravel just by being called the wrong thing. My uncle, for example. His name was *Elias*, but everyone called him *Lee* because his father had a mouth like a fish. Lee was a man who could fix anything—cars, radios, the way a broken heart might mend—but no one ever called him Elias. Not even his wife. She called him *baby* or *honey* or *you*, but never his name. And when he died, the funeral home clerk got it wrong on the headstone. They carved *Lee Elias Thompson* instead of *Elias Lee Thompson*. My mother cried for weeks. Not because of the mistake—she’d known it was a mistake—but because she realized, finally, that she’d never called him Elias. Not once.

---

I dreamt of names once. Not the usual dreams, where you’re running from something or forgetting where you are, but a dream where names were alive. They slithered like fish in a tank, silver and shimmering, and when you reached for one, it would twist away, leaving a wet trail on your fingers. I’d wake up with the taste of salt in my mouth and the knowledge that I’d been about to say something important.

I never remembered what.

---

The last time I heard my name spoken correctly was in a courtroom. The judge—a woman with a voice like gravel and a face that had seen too many lies—looked down at me and said, *"James Whitmore. You’re under arrest for the murder of Daniel Reeves."*

I didn’t deny it. I didn’t have to.

Names, I thought, are just the first step. The real work is in the forgetting.

---

Now, when I walk past a mirror, I don’t see myself. I see the ghost of a name I can’t quite remember. It’s there, just out of reach, like a word on the tip of my tongue. I press my fingers to the glass, and for a second, I swear I can feel it—*James*, *Elias*, *Lee*—all of them, tangled together like roots in the earth.

The librarian was right. I had been waiting. Not for a book, but for a name.

And now, I’m not sure I want to find it.
